title: Al-Hayy, al-Qayyum
hook: the Living, the Self-Sustaining, on whom everything rests (2:255)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawakkul, trust, and al-Wakil, the Trustee. Your line was tie the camel, then trust. Did you tie your one rope, and let the rest go? Day two hundred fifty-four.

Right now, something is holding you up. The chair. The floor under the chair. The building under the floor, the ground under the building, the planet turning under all of it, and you're not thinking about any of it. You only notice what holds you when it wobbles. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once asked a companion, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, which verse of the Qur'an is the greatest. Ubayy answered with a verse whose first line names the Living, and the one who holds everything up. And the Prophet, the hadith in Sahih Muslim says, struck him on the chest, pleased, and congratulated him on his knowledge. Today, those two names, and the first of them for our word: Al-Hayy.
screen: `WHAT'S HOLDING YOU UP?` → `THE GREATEST VERSE.` → `TWO NAMES.`

segments.voice: The verse is Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne, 2:255. In Pickthall's translation it begins: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him." The Alive is al-Hayy, from hayat, life. Muslim teachers put it this way: everything else that lives has borrowed its life and will give it back; al-Hayy's life isn't borrowed, with no start and no end. The Eternal is al-Qayyum, and here Pickthall picks one side of a rich word. It comes from q-w-m, to stand. Al-Qayyum is the One who stands by himself, needing nothing, and who keeps everything else standing. The Self-Subsisting, the Sustainer. Then comes the line that makes the names concrete: neither slumber nor sleep overtakes him. Think about what that means. Every guard falls asleep. Every parent eventually dozes off in the chair by the crib. The one holding up the heavens and the earth never does. The verse goes on: his throne, his kursi, spans the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire him. That's why it's a bedtime verse: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever recites it on going to bed has a guardian from God through the night. In that picture, the sleeper can sleep because the Sustainer doesn't. And there's a du'a from the Prophet, in at-Tirmidhi, that calls on these two names together: ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum, O Living, O Sustainer, by your mercy I seek help. Some scholars even suggested these two together are the greatest name of all.
screen: `AYAT AL-KURSI — 2:255.` · `AL-HAYY — LIFE NOT BORROWED.` · `AL-QAYYUM — KEEPS ALL STANDING.` · `NO SLUMBER, NO SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING RESTS ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit and feel what holds you up. Let your weight drop into the chair or the floor. Feel where you're touching it: your feet, your legs, your back. Let the floor take a little more of you than it usually does. Then go one layer out: the ground under the floor. Then the whole earth under that. Notice that you didn't have to hold any of it up. If you pray, you can say, quietly, ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum. The bell holds the time.
Al-Hayy. The Living, whose life is not borrowed, named together with al-Qayyum, the One who keeps everything standing. Today's word.
Your line: everything rests on him. Tonight, as you lie down, feel the bed hold you, and notice you're allowed to sleep. Day two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after each obligatory prayer and when leaving the house, and call on God as ya Hayyu ya Qayyum in times of need.

original.note: Arabic: the Living, the Self-Sustaining. hayat (life) and q-w-m (to stand).

trapdoor: what you thought: God is alive and eternal.
what it means: the Living, whose life isn't borrowed, and the one who stands alone and keeps all else standing, never sleeping.
what a scholar hears: qayyum is an intensive form from q-w-m, to stand. al-Hayy al-Qayyum appears in 2:255, 3:2 and 20:111, and some scholars proposed it as the greatest name.

sources.quoted: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 810 (Ubayy ibn Ka'b and the greatest verse)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2311 (Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime, a guardian through the night)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3524 (ya Hayyu ya Qayyum, by your mercy I seek help)
Sunan Ibn Majah 3856 (the greatest name in al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran and Ta Ha)

notes: Pickthall's 2:255 opening quoted from memory; please check word for word.
Bukhari 2311 is the story of Abu Hurayrah and the thief who taught him the verse; the script gives only its teaching. Confirm.
Whether al-Hayy al-Qayyum is the greatest name is one scholarly opinion among several; stated as 'some scholars suggested'.
